subsubtopic: REPORT ON TUNIS COMMITTEE, AND ON MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE OF O.E.C.D., IN PARIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just returned from attending the first meeting of the Canada-Tunisia Joint Committee in Tunis and the annual meeting of the Ministerial Council of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development in Paris.
I would like to table first of all the communique of the Canada-Tunisia Joint Committee which, as I said, met in Tunis from February 10 to 12. It was decided to establish this Committee at the end of President Bour-guiba's visit to Canada in May 1968. Its purpose was to reflect Canada's growing interest in its relations with the French-speaking countries of Africa in all fields.
The warm welcome which Tunisia gave to the Canadian delegation is an indication of the friendly relations between the two countries and of the favourable climate which exists for strengthening and expanding them in the future.
As a result of this meeting, Canada envisages increasing its program of economic and technical aid to Tunisia. In the year 1969-70 this aid could exceed a total of $10 million, of which $7 million would be for new initiatives, $5 million for loans on economic projects and $2 million for gifts under the expanded program of technical co-operation. In addition, we will be continuing to extend food aid to Tunisia.
In order to establish a framework which would facilitate expansion of our programs, we suggested to the Tunisians the conclusion of an agreement on economic and technical co-operation. To that end, we submitted a
draft text to be subsequently approved by the two governments.
We also discussed the possibility of concluding a trade agreement. We submitted a draft agreement to the Tunisian government in that respect. Canada intends to do the same with respect to several other African countries during the forthcoming months.
We hope of course that our aid program will pave the way for an increase in our export sales in the future.
I had an opportunity to meet with many of the Canadians working in Tunisia-there are more than 100 at present-and to see for myself one of the main activities in which we are involved, that is the children's hospital in Tunis. We have good reasons for being proud of what has been done and what is being done now by Canadians in Tunisia.
I should also like to table the communique issued at the conclusion of the meeting of the O.E.C.D. Ministerial Council which took place in Paris on February 13 and 14. This was the regular annual meeting of the ministers of O.E.C.D. countries, to review major economic trends and developments, during the past year and prospects for the months ahead.
The O.E.C.D. provides an important forum for joint consultation among the countries of Western Europe, North America and Japan over the whole range of economic policy matters, including finance and external aid. Economic conditions in these key countries have a determining influence on the growth of the world economy as a whole. Thus, the importance of close co-operation in economic and monetary policies among them cannot be over-emphasized.
The agenda for the recent meeting covered three main topics. As for the economic policy, reference was made in particular to the interdependence between international commercial and financial activities, and the need to avoid disturbances likely to affect the expansion of trade. I drew the attention of the delegates to the welcome increase in the export of capital from Europe, from which Canada has benefited in recent months.
The second topic dealt with was problems of the modern society. The O.E.C.D. will be examining in detail some of the implications

February 18, 1969
External Affairs
for economic policy arising from the rapid rate of technological progress in the industrialized world. In this connection, the delegates' attention was drawn more particularly to the growth of multinational corporations. I indicated that the questions raised by the operations of such corporations are, for Canada, of particular importance and suggested that O.E.C.D. should seek to develop internationally recognized ways and means of reconciling the various interests involved.
The third topic covered was Relations with Developing Countries, where O.E.C.D. countries also have a major role to play. I assured Canada's support for the proposed scheme of tariff preferences for the developing world and indicated the importance we attach to achieving an improvement in both the volume and the conditions of aid granted by industrialized countries.
Mr. Speaker, may I table the texts to which I referred?

I listened with great interest to the minister's comments on two quite separate matters; one of which related to relations between Canada and Tunisia, the prospect of the development of growing friendship there, and of assistance by Canada to that country. I am sure that this is something of which all Canadians would approve. This should be, of course, part of an integrated program on the part of Canada to assist in the development of so-called underdeveloped countries, particularly where we have some role to play, perhaps because of some cultural or traditional association.
With regard to O.E.C.D., again an organization of great importance to Canada, I was interested to note the emphasis that the minister placed upon the importance that Canada attached to assisting trading opportunities of underdeveloped countries. I too believe that this is of the very greatest importance. It is perhaps equal in importance to any technical or monetary assistance that might be directly offered to assist underdeveloped countries. I assure the minister and

also the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that his government would have the full support of this party in regard to efforts made to improve trading opportunities for underdeveloped countries, in terms of their trading with the developed countries of the world.

I am a little disappointed that the government of Canada, representing as it does a country with perhaps more, or at the very least as much interest in this matter as any other country of the world, is not playing a more aggressive part in the achievement of additional international monetary reform leading to increased stability.
Secondly, when we think in terms of trade I believe we should be thinking of our future options as a country. I hope that the minister and his associates will not be content simply to attend meetings such as these and to play an active part in such meetings, but that the government of Canada will accept its responsibility in terms of looking ahead to the future possible trading patterns with which Canada will be faced, and the various options that may be open to this country. For example, we should ask ourselves quite seriously whether we can continue simply to rely upon multilateral trading relations, or to what extent we might rely upon them, or to what extent we have to resort to initiatives to explore new trading patterns and possibilities.
I hope that the minister and his associates will be giving these problems-monetary reform, future trading patterns, and the future of Canada in connection with both- their very closest attention.

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, February 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Benson that Bill C-165, to amend the Income Tax Act and the Estate Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Saltsman (p. 5191).

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has made much of the fact that he has agreed to changes in his original proposal in regard to estate taxation. But these changes were minor modifications only. There is no basic difference between the legislation we are considering today and the original measure outlined by the minister almost four months ago. He set out then to destroy any accumulation of private capital that remained in this country. His intent is still the same. All he did was change the load in the murder weapon. It may take the family farm and small private Canadian business a little longer to die under the new arrangement, but they are just as surely doomed to extinction now as they were when the minister passed sentence on them back last October.
There is one aspect of the minister's behaviour in this whole affair which I must confess I am at a loss to understand. I refer to the atmosphere of deception and trickery in which he has cloaked all his announcements and explanations. Nothing could be more devious than the way in which he has sought to confuse the public and convince Canadians that he has really done them a great favour by the latest changes in his proposal.
The minister implied, although he was careful not to spell it out, that Canadians would now enjoy an estate tax exemption of $50,000 instead of the originally announced $20,000. When we read the fine print, however, we see that what he did was leave the old exemption of $20,000 unchanged. He merely raised the tax floor to $50,000. What this means is that if a man dies leaving an estate of $50,000 he is exempt from the estate tax. But if he is unfortunate enough to have been $1,000 more successful and to have left an estate of $51,000, his estate will be liable to taxation and the exemption will be only $20,000. In other words, it would be liable to the new punitive tax rates on a sum of $31,000.
February 18, 1969

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act
Anyone who knows the value of real estate in the province of Ontario today, and who appreciates the inflated value of everything, thanks to the Liberal 60-cent dollar, knows very well that a prosperous family farm or a thriving small business will more than likely be well within the minister's taxing grasp. All he has done by setting the arbitrary figure of $50,000 is to assure that those family farms, small businesses and other family concerns which are efficient and most valuable to the economy will be hardest hit.
The minister has succeeded very neatly in penalizing efficiency. He has hit the very bracket of private business which contributes most to the national economy. The marginal farm, the ineffective manager, the part-time enterprise that needs either moonlighting or other outside assistance to stay alive, have been placed in a preferred position. For the time being at least they will escape the tax axe, if they carry the Benson seal of inefficiency. But the family farm operated by a trained and dedicated farmer will be desperately hard hit. The grocery store, the garage, the local automobile or farm machinery outlet, or any other type of rural Ontario family enterprise which is effectively run as a family business, will get the full cut.
If the minister is sincere in his explanation of this tax, why is he risking the ruin of a large and lively section of our national economy for the sake of a paltry $30 million in revenue? And $30 million is a paltry amount of tax money to those who can shrug off underestimates in national budgeting running into thousands of millions. It is a paltry amount to a minister who countenances an increase of more than $1 billion in national spending in one year while at the same time preaching austerity and restraint in spending.
In a speech some time ago at London the minister said there had been very few cases of businesses or family farms having to be sold to meet taxation. What he failed to mention was that this has been true in the past; it was only true in the days before the coming into effect of his new proposals. He also failed to mention that the actual sale of family businesses or farms would normally take place before the death of the owner, though the chief motive for selling out would still be the menace of the estate tax.
In the Montreal Gazette of January 29 the highly respected financial writer, John Meyer, touches on this point. He wrote as follows:
The exemption of all estates up to $100,000 would cost the government, according to some estimates, only $12 million in revenue while permitting large

savings In processing. Such an exemption would relieve many of the small business and farm difficulties raised by the present taxing process. It would substantially relieve the forced sales which are a particular objection to estate taxation generally. That advantage could be achieved at quite a small cost if Mr. Benson would be prepared to recognize it. Mr. Benson, however, says the experience of the finance department indicated that forced sales after death to meet taxes are limited. No doubt this is true. What neither Mr. Benson or the finance department can possibly know is the number of sales made in advance of death. The tax consultants and professional executors could have told him if given the chance.
No, Mr. Speaker, the minister has not really changed anything. He has juggled some figures and reworded a few press releases but he has kept intact the punitive quality of his legislation. Private enterprise and private initiative are to be discouraged. The minister has made them an offence and he has provided penalties which are harsh, discriminatory and destructive.
The message of this government-this government of the just society, publicly pledged to the support of individual rights and freedom-as broadcast by the Minister of Finance is clear. It is: Get out of the field of private endeavour. Sell your store, sell your business, sell your farm. Move to the city and get a job where we can keep our eye on you and deduct our taxes at source. Become part of the regimented mass and do not foul up our computers with individual initiative. Or, as one of my constituents put it the other day: Sell off all your holdings now, blow the proceeds in high living in Florida and Europe and return broke to live the rest of your lives on welfare.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
Before I finish my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say something about one of the most arbitrary and unjust aspects of this taxation. As a matter of fact, it is an aspect that is part of all federal taxation. This is the fact that the federal authority levies taxes upon individual Canadians and individual Canadian enterprises at its own valuation.
I am sure there are very few members in this house who have not learned first hand of examples of this inequity. The federal valuation is too often made at long range and without any regard to local valuation or the effect of temporary or long-term economic recession on those local valuations. Under the proposed estate tax scheme it will be quite possible for families sincerely to believe that they are well under the taxation floor only to find that an arbitrary federal valuation places them not

only in a taxable bracket but well up in it. This has happened in the past and is even more likely to happen under this proposed scheme. Then just watch the forced sale of farms and businesses to meet estate taxes.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that most members, like myself, find it rather hard to believe that the finance minister has had, to use his own words, very few protests in regard to the proposed changes in the estate tax legislation. In view of the tremendous number of letters that have been received by most members from all across the country, the taxpayers of Canada must either be unaware of the minister's presence in the house or feel that his attitude is so stubborn and inflexible that it would be useless for them to appeal either to his good nature or to his good judgment.
Personally, I cannot recall a single issue that has brought forth such a volume of mail from my constituents. I know too that many other members have received the same tidal wave of protest. The remarkable thing about all this mail is that it comes from individuals who are concerned and is not part of an organized effort. Surely even the minister of a government as arrogant and as far removed from the thinking of the people as this one cannot long remain totally unaware of the massive resistance to this measure that continues to grow daily from coast to coast.
I want to be fair to the minister. Ey exempting an inheritance between spouses from taxation he has recognized the contribution both partners in a marriage make toward building a common estate. But what he fails to recognize is that the one main incentive for such a partnership is the creation of something tangible to pass on to their offspring. This legislation makes it virtually impossible to pass on a viable family economic unit intact to the heirs without involving them in an undue amount of debt.
I am concerned about the effect of this negative and destructive tax on the Canadian economy and the Canadian society as a whole. Representing a rural riding as I do, I am

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act particularly concerned about its effect on Canada's agricultural community, the independent rural businessmen and farmers. In the past it has been difficult enough to establish sons on the family farm. The minister in a speech to a Liberal meeting admitted that the estate tax places a burden on the transfer of family farms and businesses between generations, but he suggested the burden is not a heavy one.
He went on to say that an estate tax does place a special burden on estates in which the major assets are not liquid, which is almost always the case when a farm or business is owned and operated as a family enterprise. The burden, he said, is only significant where the business is to be carried on by the children, or has not been sold at the time of death of the chief shareholder. In other words, he has admitted that the tax is going to make it difficult to continue small family enterprises. He has further admitted it by changing his original proposals in two ways: first, estates under $50,000 will be tax exempt and, second, instalment payments of the tax will be allowed up to five years. Even with these changes he does not grapple with the situation in which the taxes are levied on the basis of an arbitrary valuation of the property, or where such valuations do not bear any resemblance to local market conditions or take into account regional economic cycles.
Let me give an illustration. A farm in Manitoba which could have been sold for $250 an acre last year would, because of the surplus grain situation, shortage of cash and high interest rates, be hard to sell at the present time at any price. It is not unlikely that any family farm in western Canada could be greatly over valuated under those conditions and have to be sacrificed at a valuation far below that placed upon it by the federal tax authorities.
Inflated costs, particularly of machinery and equipment, have placed all but the smallest farm enterprise well over the $50,000 valuation. With inflation still rampant the minister has caught a huge number of small family businesses and farm enterprises in a tax net originally designed to catch only the very largest. In fact, he has left the largest estates virtually untouched and hit out hard at the smaller ones. This is in line with other actions of this government such as the preferred position given people with higher incomes in the application of the new 2 per cent social development tax.

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act
Nor does the exemption up to $50,000 do much to change the situation. A more realistic exemption base under present inflated conditions would be $100,000. The fact that the tax exemption for estates over $50,000 still remains at $20,000 simply proves that the minister has not taken the time or trouble to study the serious effects the application of the tax will have on our free enterprise system. One does not have to be an economist to realize that all this will lead to the phasing out of the family enterprise and the emergence of corporate groups. It means the extinction of the family farm, and inevitably of Canada's agricultural communities.
The Western Producer had this to say in a recent editorial:
It is almost incredible that the government that has had so much to say about the "just society" should introduce such punitive legislation. It seems to us there could be no quicker way to destroy the family farm and to hasten the day when land resources will be controlled by huge corporations.
When one considers that 75 per cent of estate taxes collected by the federal government goes to the provinces, I say it is just as incredible that discussions were not held with the provinces before imposition of the tax. This is particularly so since the federal share amounts to approximately one per cent of the federal budget. Of this amount it is estimated the government would lose $12 million if all estates below $100,000 were exempt, as my hon. friend from Victoria-Haliburton noted. At the same time there would be a considerable saving in not having to process the greater number of estates involved. One wonders, under these conditions, if this new estate tax set-up is being brought in not as an economic measure but rather as a social measure.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Surely this levelling off in the distribution of wealth need not reach down to penalize thrifty, independent businessmen and farmers who, in a lifetime, use their earnings to build modest estates for themselves and their families. It is of interest to read what the Ontario Economic Council had to say in its report just prior to the estate tax changes announced as part of the current budget. I quote from that part of the report which is most apt:
Those responsible for guiding the course of our nation's development need only to look to history to find proof that nearly every past civilization has hastened its ruin through dissipation of capital by taxation.

One has only to read the history of the Roman empire to see what economic oppression of the individual farmer and businessman can do to hasten this ruin. There the small farmers and small businessmen were driven from their holdings to become faceless parts of an urban mob that contributed nothing and demanded everything.
In a country such as Canada that is hungry for capital and counts capital as one of its largest imports, one would think the formation and development of private capital within the country would be the government's foremost aim. Among 14 countries surveyed by the Ontario Economic Council, Canada was found to levy the highest percentage of tax on capital. It was ahead of the United States and Great Britain by a wide margin; it was even ahead of socialist Sweden. Canada was third of ten nations in the percentage of total government revenue raised by death duties and gift taxation. Great Britain was first at 3 per cent; the U.S. was next with 2.6 per cent and Canada was third with 1.8 per cent. West Germany, last with 0.1 per cent, had the lowest rate of estate tax but showed the highest rate of economic growth. That may be significant.
One other aspect of the proposed estate tax worth nothing is the supposed concession to wives contained in the new regulations. The Canadian Tax Foundation dismissed this point by saying it was simply "a carrot dangled before wives" that could and probably would lead to unexpected tax pitfalls. The truth of the matter is that it is no concession at all. It is simply a deferral of taxation. And when the tax bite comes later it will be that much sharper and deeper. This deferred tax only means eventual taxation at higher rates.
This is far more a social measure than an economic one. When one considers how little revenue will be forthcoming and when one further considers that the minister did not bother to consult the provinces about a matter that so intimately concerned them, one is forced to conclude his objective was something other than revenue raising.
In the Hamilton Spectator, as quoted in the Winnipeg Tribune of January 11, the editorial writer notes:
Not only does its underlying motive appear to be directed more towards a theoretical political aim than to a fiscal need, but the measure could radically change the character and purpose of Canadian business.
The editorial concludes:
Surplus capital essential to Canadian ownership and to industrial expansion in this country is

being increasingly diverted into government coffers. In the years to come these estate tax measures will change the economic and social structure of Canada.
May I also quote an article in the same issue of the Winnipeg Tribune:
Mr. Benson's basic assumption in the draft law is that a man has really no right to direct how his savings are to be used after his death. In Mr. Benson's philosophy a man's life earnings become the property of the government and anything he disposes of by will is allowed only by government benevolence.
With all that I agree, Mr. Speaker. But perhaps the editorial writer laid the blame in the wrong place. I do not believe this is the philosophy of the Minister of Finance. I think that this is the basic philosophy of the so-called "just society". He had no choice except to do his master's bidding. As the Winnipeg Tribune writer put it:
This is, of course, arrant statism and authoritarianism at its worst.
That is not a bad description of this "just society" we are supposed to be enjoying.
I return to the point I made earlier about the family unit and the motivation of the family partnership. On this point and on the whole question of the direction in which the Prime Minister's "just society" is leading us, I recommend most highly to hon. members that they read an article in the Winnipeg Free Press of December 2, 1968, by Shaun Herron. In part he says:
-the impulse to prosper and provide, to "do the best one can for one's family", this we have approved, this we preach, this we applaud. And, of course, what a man makes is his. He pays his taxes on it-and today they are heavy-but what he has left after taxes is the fruit of his work, skill, foresight, and enterprise. It is his, earned and paid for by blood, sweat, toil and taxes-
Has it occurred to Mr. Trudeau that when he forces men, who can, who will, and who want to work hard, to ask "why work?" he has begun the creation of a "just" society in which all men are equally grey, equally poor, equally idle and equally ill? Is this what the Liberal caucus intended?
After that, Mr. Speaker, there is little to add. I simply say that the proposed new estate tax system is unjust, unnecessary and unrewarding. If it has been conceived as an economic measure it will do harm to the economy, not good; it will cause far-reaching economic disaster and will remain a monument to the negative and the destructive. If it is advanced as a social measure in disguise, then I believe it to be unwarranted and exceedingly dangerous to all those beliefs and
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act institutions on which our country has been built and which have enabled it to prosper.
I hope that the minister and the government will consider dropping this tax on death, particularly since it applies to moderate family enterprises. I am speaking of independent businessmen and farmers who have contributed so much to our basic philosophy of freedom and who, if allowed to survive, will remain the backbone of our free enterprise system.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this estate tax measure I wish to say that this problem has been debated long and inconclusively by many people. No doubt governments need money; the public purse must be filled in as many ways as possible. But the amount of tax that needs to be raised depends on the spending habits of the government and the demands of society for social programs and money to carry out those programs.
Any single tax measure in a taxation system is introduced as a result of many social, economic and other factors of long standing. It is considered that an undue concentration of wealth resulting from a complete absence of transfer taxes tends to destroy the incentive that makes the economy viable. On the other hand, too severe an imposition of transfer taxes has the same effect; it reduces the national urge to save and build. It can be argued with a reasonable degree of righteousness that it is socially desirable to introduce estate taxes which will prevent the build-up of large units of economic family wealth. It is argued that such accumulated units of wealth do not serve the interests of society generally and ought not to be allowed to remain intact.
The bulk of tax revenue comes from taxation of income and consumption. Transfer taxes, or estate taxes, are levied nationally on accumulations of capital. As such they naturally influence the behaviour of the individual bearing the brunt of this tax. The citizens who are most directly concerned about this problem and who have been very vocal in their objections are farmers and small businessmen. They have been so vocal that the Minister of Finance has seen fit to change the provisions of the estate tax regulations. As a result some relief has been given to these people.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The imposition of the estate tax on larger estates has meant that on the death of the
5652	COMMONS
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act Canadian investor there has been a movement to sell many businesses to foreign firms, especially to United States firms. In a country which is continually worried about the substantial foreign capital investment and which must rely for a high degree of capital inflow either on the savings of its own people or on foreign investment, tax policies that encourage the sale of businesses to foreign investors should be seriously considered by the nation as a whole in the light of whether or not the estate tax is a good tax.
The recent statement of the three prairie premiers in which they urged that the fiscal policy of the federal government should take priority over the language question at the Federal-provincial conference last week indicates the very great concern of these premiers and of many people in Canada that the strains of our nation's fiscal problems could well contribute to our break-up and the fragmentation of the political life of the country. These same premiers have signified their intention of remitting the provinces' portion of the estate tax to estates, which indicates their feeling that the estate tax needs radical revision.
The estate tax falls upon the family of the entrepreneur whose enterprise has created the capital while his family has had to undergo social and economic restrictions. It might be socially desirable that all income and revenue should revert to the Crown on the death of the entrepreneur but such an attitude would, I am sure, prevent or seriously discourage enterprise by individual entrepreneurs.
In a report of the Ontario Economic Council, of 14 countries examined Canada emerged with the highest general capital taxes, including death taxes, gift and property taxes, surpassing the United States and Great Britain. It is significant that Germany had a low estate tax and a high rate of economic growth compared with Britain where there was a high death tax rate and very low economic growth. The study asks: "Are our estate tax laws designed to chastise or to welcome investors and job creators?" In my opinion the rather violent reaction engendered by the minister's estate tax formula is generally the result of the inflationary period through which we have passed and which we will likely continue to experience for a number of the years.
The minister has stated that 95 per cent of Canadians will not be involved in estate tax.
I suggest that the percentage will be much less than he has forecast and that in the

DEBATES	February 18, 1969
future many more people will be involved inasmuch as once this legislation is on the statute books it will not be changed for a number of years. Even with the proviso that estates of $50,000 or less will not be taxed, in the near future many more estates will be taxed and the numbers will grow in volume even though the real value remains constant owing to the inflationary change.
Indeed, unless most farms and small businesses have capital of over $50,000 they will not provide for their owners any reasonable degree of standard of living. The capitalization on western farms, in order to return the owner $5,000 or $6,000 a year even including the operator's wages, needs to be in the order of $60,000 to $100,000. The general philosophy of the farmer and small businessman in his earlier years was to save money out of his income to build up his business so he would have more to retire on or to pass on to his family. In recent years the Canadian economic climate has not been directed at all toward the building up of savings for the farmer and small businessman to pay off their obligations. We have become a very consumptive type of society in which we are projecting a philosophy that everyone is entitled to consume without the corresponding proviso that he should produce.
Regardless of the perhaps basic philosophy that all personal resources should return to the estate on the individual's death, I believe we are overlooking one very important factor that bas not received much consideration or debate by our people. It has been said by many that automation will replace many people in the manufacture of the products we consume, but a recent study by the Economic Council of Canada in its fifth annual review would indicate that we are moving steadily into an economy that is becoming increasingly service-oriented. A service-oriented economy is a difficult area in which to establish a high level of efficiency. For instance, in the United States last year the health service field was considered to be the third largest industry, with the projection that it would become the largest industry within a few years.
The service field is an area where it is increasingly difficult to carry out an efficient operation. The Canadian Economic Council's analysis of changes in the growth pattern of the Canadian economy discloses a really amazing trend. In the period from 1946 to 1966 Canada experienced an enormous expansion and diversification of industrial activity,
February 18, 1969

but the more striking fact is that all the employment growth took place in the service industries. While the shares of the goods producing and service producing sections have remained approximately constant in value of output-each section accounting for roughly 50 per cent throughout the period-the shares in terms of employment have changed places.
In 1946 the goods producing industries accounted for about 60 per cent of total employment; in 1966 tjie service producing industries accounted for about 60 per cent. In the goods producing industries real output expanded about 5 per cent annually while employment did not expand at all, so that the real growth was about 5 per cent annually per worker. In the service industries real output expanded more than 4 per cent annually but employment grew almost as fast and the growth rate of output per worker was only about 1 per cent annually.
In western Europe the service industries account for only about 35 per cent of the employment as opposed to 60 per cent in Canada. This creates a marked imbalance in growth rates between the economies of Canada and western Europe and if carried forward could result in difficulties for our economy. This means that we must look increasingly for greater efficiency in our economy.
I believe it is becoming more and more important that t,he small individual entrepreneur be encouraged to remain and increase his stake in the economic growth of the country, and that our society would be sadly lacking if it attempted to dispense with these people. Management is very important in our economy. Indeed, management is just as important as labour, and unless the two are very closely joined labour is unable to progress without good management. The fact that farm management has increased its efficiency faster than any other part of our economy in the past two decades indicates that the individual farmer is as efficient as his large industrial counterpart. Indeed, an analysis of the position of the Soviet Union shows that relatively many more people are needed to work in agriculture in that country than in North America to produce the food needed to feed the country. The Economic Council suggests that larger farms, new technology, better inputs and research in agriculture are necessary to raise productivity in food production, processing and distribution.
It is my contention, Mr. Speaker, that the estate tax will work to discourage individual
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act initiative and saving, at least in the lower strata of those who will be paying the state taxes. Consider the man of 50, either a small businessman or farmer, who has been moderately successful. He sees an opportunity to expand but realizes that perhaps he should decide that the accumulation of wealth is not worth the worry, the saving and the reducing of his standard of living so that he may expand his business. So he remains at his present economic level, takes a trip to Hawaii or does some other spending in a consumptive way. Yet in the 50-70 age group are often found many of the best managers in our economy. We are the poorer if these entrepreneurs suddenly decide that work, worry and striving only bring trouble with the income tax department or with estate tax in the event of his death. I believe we cannot stress too strongly that the individual entrepreneur is a very important part of our financial picture and contributes greatly to our economic efficiency as a society. The estate tax in its present form is retrogressive.
It is well known that there is another aspect of this tax that is not quite realized. It is an expensive tax to collect from the government's point of view and it is costly to the estate to present its case. In many smaller estates where the tax revenue is small the cost of collecting is greater than the tax received by the treasury. To present its side of the case the estate in turn has to hire expensive accountants, lawyers, etc., all of whom must be paid. This further reduces the value of the estate and is eventually a loss to the whole community and country.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
It is a tax where there are many grey areas, where inspectors far removed from the scene of the estate often over value. Indeed, it is very difficult to evaluate much property in small communities where real estate may sell very infrequently and land values may vary by 50 per cent in a year, or in a mile. The estate tax often attempts to tax goodwill in a business when it is advantageous to the tax department. But the breakdown value may be much less and the heirs to the estate may choose to cease business or, if possible, sell the business. To sell to another Canadian only increases his estate problems on his death, and the logical choice is to sell to foreign capital, usually American.
I do not believe it is by accident that the three prairie provinces are the ones that are in the process of rebating the federal portion
February 18, 1969

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act of the estate tax revenues. The prairies do not want to accept any measure which might slow their resource development. They have no basic concern about the origins of capital that will pour into those provinces for the development of petroleum, mineral and other resources. The economic nationalism to be found in the east is foreign to the prairies. The contrast between the free trading west and the protectionist east is as old as confederation itself. It has been lessened somewhat by the tariff reductions since the end of the war, but much difference of thought lies between those who live by the exploitation of resources and those who manufacture.
We must consider this tax in our federal approach to the constitutional issue. The economic forces in Canada tend to divide rather than unite. In its approach to the estate tax the federal government is pursuing a policy that is basically not in keeping with the aims and aspirations of the western provinces and the fundamental pull of the economic forces under which they operate.
This bill is largely a reform of the existing estate tax law. It is too bad that in his wisdom the minister did not increase the exemption in line with the rapid rise of inflation to a position where the application of estate taxes would have some relation in real money to what the levels were 15 or 20 years ago. It is my contention that the tax starts too low and is graduated too steeply. I would hope the minister would consider this and make the appropriate changes in the bill before it is finally passed.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are engaged in a discussion about two of the most sombre facts of existence-death and taxes. Such a discussion is sombre enough in itself but this one has been rendered all the more difficult, and I might even say more horrendous, by the vast degree of exaggeration and misrepresentation which have characterized discussion of the government's proposal. One would think from the remarks we have heard this afternoon that even the beneficient parts of the proposal would be opposed by members of the opposition parties. For example, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Muir) can only be said to have damned with faint praise the proposal that bequests and gifts to widows be exempt, and I would like to see how he and his colleagues will vote on that.
We suggest that the changes which are proposed by the bill are in the national

interest and will not bear heavily on any significant section of the Canadian economy. I speak on this bill as one who represents a constituency which can be said to be approximately 50 per cent rural and 50 per cent urban. There is no question in my mind that the urban dwellers in Canada approve wholeheartedly the changes which are proposed.
We live in a society which all of us like to believe can be described as one where a large degree of equality of opportunity prevails. We live in a society where all of us would like to believe that it is the worth of the individual, his effort and his own competence which will lead him to success in life. We live in a society where most people like to believe that a man is judged by what he is, not who he is, not whose son he is.
When I hear some of the comments that are made by hon. members opposite I wonder whether they are opposing this bill or are opposing estate taxes and succession duties as such. This is not at all clear from many things that have been said. I do not think that the people of this country require public men to apologize for the fact that taxes are levied on estates. The time has long since gone when this was a discussible or debatable proposition.
Certainly there is no strong determining mood in this country to confiscate wealth or to confiscate estates, but I think it is the feeling of the great majority of Canadians that we should not live in a society where large blocks of inherited wealth are passed on from generation to generation to the detriment of many people who are not in the fortunate position of sharing in that inherited wealth, and none of us who support this bill, nor public men who through the years have supported estate taxes and succession duties, need apologize for the position that has been taken.
The essential parts of the present proposal have been described many times in this chamber. On the one hand, the government has proposed that bequests and gifts of all kinds to wives and, indeed, to husbands should be tax exempt and, on the other hand, the government has proposed that to make good the loss of revenue that has occurred there be adjustments elsewhere in the tax structure.
It is significant for all of us here to realize that we are not the only country which is giving consideration to changes in tax policy. For example, as we all know there has recently been a change in the administration
February 18, 1969	COMMONS
in the United States. Last week it was announced in the New York Times that serious thought is being given by the treasury department in the United States to the adoption of the very types of proposals which have been made to us in this parliament, that gifts and bequests to wives be exempted from taxation and that as a countervailing measure there be a stiller rate of tax on gifts inter vivos and a higher rate throughout the estate tax structure. Incidentally, with reference to a table produced, I think, by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) or perhaps it was the hon. member for Lisgar, that there is very little difference in the incidence of estate tax in the United States and in Canada in percentage terms, and it would be very hard for anybody to say that the American economy is stagnant and has been made so by estate taxes.
I think I am not unique in this chamber in having participated in a large number of discussions with my constituents about the incidence of the new estate tax. As I said a moment ago, there is no question that the changes have been widely accepted in the urban part of my constituency where the predominant interest is that of the public service, but because of the exaggerated and inflammatory discussion about the consequences of this tax which appeared in certain farm newspapers I found to my very great surprise that some farmers in my constituency had become inordinately alarmed about what would happen if this tax measure were passed. I thought it might be of some interest to hon. members if I were to relate some of the things I have said to my constituents which bear upon the concern expressed in rural Canada about the incidence and implications of this tax.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
One thing which struck me immediately was that many farmers spoke as if this was the first time estate taxes or succession duties had been applied in this country. As we know, of course, this is not so. I cannot speak for all the provinces but in the province of Ontario succession duties or inheritance taxes have been collected by the provincial government since 1892. Everybody here knows that the dominant interest of government in the estate tax or succession duty field has been provincial. It was not until 1941 that the federal government entered the succession duty and estate tax field. This was done at that
DEBATES	5655
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act time as part of a series of wartime tax agreements under which the provinces in effect rented certain of their taxing jurisdiction to the federal government.
In the discussion which has taken place on this measure it has frequently been said by spokesmen on this side of the house that the provincial interest in estate taxes remains predominant. In the province of Ontario approximately 75 per cent of the taxes paid on death go to the provincial government and only 25 per cent go to the federal government. This is a fact which seems to be greatly overlooked by many critics, particularly critics on the other side of the house who I think might support the present provincial government.
I have before me a table I have prepared showing the comparative incidence of Ontario succession duties, the present estate tax and the proposed estate tax. It is based upon what, from the standpoint of the new estate tax, is the most difficult assumption, namely, a father leaving the whole of his estate to only one adult son. This corresponds with the case put by so many farmers that they intend in one way or another to pass the whole of their estate to one son so that the farm can be carried on in the farm family.
If the estate is valued at $50,000 no Ontario succession duty tax is paid, no tax is payable under the present estate tax and no tax is payable under the proposed estate tax. If the estate is valued at $100,000 the Ontario succession duty amounts to $7,910, the present estate tax amounts to $5,100 and the proposed estate tax amounts to $6,600. If the estate is valued at $150,000 the Ontario succession duty would amount to $13,950, the present estate tax would amount to $10,700 and the proposed estate tax would amount to $13,350. If the estate is valued at $200,000 the Ontario succession duty would take 20,348, the present estate tax would take $16,800 and the proposed estate tax would take $21,600.
These figures lead all of us to certain important conclusions. The first is that many farmers in this province obviously are unaware of the nature of their estate tax liability. It is clear that many people with whom I have spoken personally were completely unaware of the fact that for estates up to $100,000 under the present and proposed estate tax more money would be taken by the Ontario succession duty than by the federal estate tax.
Another thing which I found extraordinary, and which we all must recognize as a fact, is that many farmers in my constituency, and I
5656	COMMONS
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act have no doubt elsewhere in the country, were completely unaware ol the total level of their liability for their estate. Let me, for example, quote again the incidence of tax on an estate of $100,000. The Ontario succession duty would amount to $7,900, the present estate tax would amount to $5,100, and the net tax would be $13,000. Under the proposed estate tax it would be increased by $1,500.
Many people with whom I spoke felt that for the first time they were to be taxed under this proposal when in fact they were already taxed at a high level and the added tax is relatively small. The discussion on this matter in the province of Ontario has been complicated by the fact that many people have been unaware of the present provision in the federal Estate Tax Act which is being carried forward that a tax credit of 50 per cent is given to the taxpayer in recognition of the fact that he has to pay Ontario succession duty. I, and I am sure other hon. members, have seen Ontario publications which have recited what was alleged to be the tax payable under this proposal in this province but which have failed to take into account the fact that the tax is reduced by 50 per cent by reason of the fact that Ontario succession duty is payable.
I should say that the figures I have quoted are net figures making allowance for the 50 per cent tax credit. I have found that the initial concern of farmers in my constituency, and I believe in eastern Ontario, about the proposed tax changes has been to an almost complete extent allayed and removed as a result of further study and consideration. The attempt which some people have made, whether intentionally or not-someone has said intentionally; I hope that is not so but it could be-to portray this tax as if it were a new imposition completely different in kind and character from anything farmers or businessmen have ever experienced before has been dissipated, I think, by the knowledge which has come from greater study of this measure.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It is my belief that no farmer who in any way could be described as an average farmer in this province is put in a perilous position by the tax change. It is my considered opinion that this tax will not have any of the horrendous effects which have been ascribed to it. The headlines which have appeared in farm newspapers to the effect that the new

DEBATES	February 18, 1969
estate tax will doom the family farm are simply untrue and cannot be substantiated by the facts. In fact, I would go so far as to say that the making of this change in estate tax law will produce an unintended benefit for many farmers and businessmen.
I repeat again that a large number of people were simply unaware of the fact that they were exposed to a very substantial degree of taxation under the existing law. They now realize what their existing tax liabilities were, and many of them for the first time are turning their attention to ways and means of reorganizing their affairs in order to lessen the incidence and burden of taxation. I need not tell hon. members that there are many ways in which farmers in particular can reorganize their farm business to their own advantage and in such a fashion as to lessen the incidence of taxation. I say in answer to those concerned about the incidence of estate tax that this change to a considerable extent will be beneficial to many farmers.
Although no one welcomes tax changes, it is easier to live with them when we can see, as we do here, that the main change will provide a beneficial relief to widows from the burden of estate tax. second reading and reference to the Standing Committee on regional development of Bill C-20, to establish a National Capital Region Planning Board.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to introduce Bill C-20 entitled: "An Act to establish a National Capital Region Planning Board".
Last week, for instance, the future of Canada's provincial capital was settled at the federal-provincial conference. It was proposed to create a capital unequaled in the whole world, a capital made up of the twin cities of Ottawa and Hull, a bilingual capital, the capital of a federal state.
This bill is intended to establish for this region a planning board, which is under discussion at the present time and which has not been determined as yet. It is in the spirit of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said last week that I introduce this bill this afternoon.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I present a bill which is designed to call attention to something which is absolutely essential if we are going to build thk kind of national capital we have in mind. Last week at the federal-provincial conference a tripartite committee was established of federal officials and provincial officials of Quebec and Ontario to carry forward a series of technical discussions.
Our Canadian national capital, such as it is apparently agreed we will create, will be one without parallel in any other part of the world. It will be a national capital with part in the province of Quebec, with its primary use of the French language, with its own educational institutions, with its own code of property and civil law, and part in the province of Ontario with a different code of property and civil law, with a different educational system and with the primary use of the English language. There is no question that the task of combining the cities of Ottawa and Hull into a functioning federal capital will be a great challenge to Canadians and
February 18, 1969

one which will be the subject of many discussions before it is completed.
I think it is particularly appropriate at this stage that we should have a debate in this place to concern ourselves with some of the absolutely fundamental things that must be decided before we can proceed to build the capital we all want to see. My bill this afternoon calls attention to only one aspect of the problem, that is, the creation of a planning board which will include part of the province of Quebec and part of the province of Ontario within the spirit with which there was general agreement at the federal-provincial conference.
The problems are very complex, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to outline some general features of them. First, there is the problem of resolving the conflicts over land use and traffic arteries. At this stage the province of Ontario has created a regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton. This has brought a measure of rationalization to the Ontario side of this region which was long overdue. We certainly anticipate that on the Quebec side the 30-odd municipalities involved in the area which seems to be under discussion can be unified through some type of parallel legislation, and there is every evidence that this is under close examination by the Quebec authorities. Then the problem will be to bring together the planners of one side of the river and the planners of the other side of the river.
We are aware of the delicate constitutional problems and do not wish in any respect to minimize them, but surely the very first step must be to bring together in some kind of advisory board representatives of the province of Quebec, the province of Ontario, the federal government and the municipalities concerned. It will be essential, in my opinion, that there be an informal and advisory function at least in the beginning, no more than that, in order that the parties may get to know each other, in order that they can hire the necessary staff to serve the purposes they have in mind, in order to resolve some absolutely essential priorities.
I can think of the new bridges that certainly have to be built over the Ottawa River, but there has been a serious question in my mind whether a bridge for public transit purposes should not have a prior claim over a bridge designed to serve private automobiles. My colleague, the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle), who I hope will be speaking in this debate, certainly has some very interesting 29180-359

National Capital Commission proposals in the field of public transportation, and I am sure these will be examined by the appropriate authorities in the near future.
But, Mr. Speaker, the task of bringing them together is only the first challenge. The second challenge is to somehow, in some kind of orderly way that makes sense, bring a degree of supervision over these functions and a co-ordination of them. This I hope will be the task of the National Capital Commission which was created by act of this parliament and which functions sometimes, I may say, with doubtful constitutional jurisdiction in the area which it considers its primary responsibility, that is, the planning of land use in the national capital region and, if I may say so, the constitutional problem with respect to property and civil rights makes its task not a very easy one. Somehow the role of the National Capital Commission has to be fitted into the planning authority that we propose to create. I am not at all sure that my proposal of 11 members, with the chairman from the N.C.C., five from Ontario and five from Quebec, is the precise answer. I offer it merely as a suggestion of the kind of formula that may be discussed and decided. The numbers might be varied, but I think it would be a useful principle if the chairman of such a planning board were a member of the National Capital Commission because the National Capital Commission is almost the sole agency in a position to look at the whole region in order to take the large view, in order to make the kind of suggestions that we hope will be observed by the municipalities and the provinces.
This is the season of the year when many things begin to stir in our very beautiful national capital region, a region which I think is one of the most beautiful in the world. It is going through the late stages of winter and very soon we will see the springtime. Problems debated in this house in previous years in springtime have followed a very regular and not particularly brilliant pattern.
I see my hon. friend, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), in his seat on the other side of the house. For the last four or five years I have followed his springtime incursions into the pothole problem. He looks into his files and pulls out the problem of the condition of Ottawa streets and potholes, and usually he has a television presentation on this matter. Then there is the suggestion that members of this house could do a better job of running municipalities. That has very frequently been mentioned by hon. members

Mr. Speaker, the bill which has been brought forward by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) is a valuable means of rivetting the attention of this house and indeed the attention of the whole country upon the problems of the Ottawa area.
As one who came to Ottawa to live some 18 or 19 years ago, I believe that the discussions as to the relationship between the municipalities in this area and the federal government have not always been of a proper order, nor have they been carried on, in my opinion, in a proper manner. In my view there has been far too much recrimination, too much of one authority blaming the other, too much confusion and inaction resulting from conflicts between municipalities, provincial governments and the federal government. I say that the worse thing any of us could do in this chamber at the present time would be to perpetuate the nonsense implicit in this ancient manner of talking about our capital.
We are faced here with a problem of immense magnitude. In this area at the present time there are perhaps less than 400,000 people. It is estimated that some time after 1980 there will be over a million people in the area. Unless all the government agencies and other authorities concerned take the necessary steps to look ahead and plan for the future we shall indeed be faced with grave problems. All participants in the conference agreed to a resolution which I think it is proper to record here:
1.	The Constitutional Conference is agreed that the cities of Ottawa and Hull are the core of the Canadian capital area.
2.	No changes be made to provincial boundaries or to the constitutional responsibilities of the governments concerned.
3.	The boundaries of the Canadian capital area are to be established by agreement of the governments concerned.

5.	That the Study Committee on the Canadian capital continue its work giving particular importance to the following:
(a)	the definition of suburban areas which would eventually constitute, along with the cities of Ottawa and Hull, the Canadian capital regions;
(b)	a study of the administration and the financing of the tripartite organization.

When the proposals were originally put forward I must say frankly that I did not agree with them in total. At that time I felt that no estate under $50,000 should be taxed. Since that time many hon. members have suggested the exemption should be $100,000. However, I think they are wrong. I do not believe the average working man in Canada would accept a $100,000 exemption or minimum upon which taxes would be paid. Taxes not only have to be just, but they must appear to be just. I think many people in Canada would feel $100,000 would be far too high to give any pretence of justice.
The previous speaker suggested that taxing estates of $50,000 would be completely unrealistic. I would point out that if a man wishes to leave his farm to his children, $50,000 could be left to his wife as a gift which would not be taxable, and $50,000 could be left to his children which would not be taxable because of the floor in the taxation plan. In effect, such a farmer could leave $100,000 without any tax being paid, $50,000 tax free to his wife and $50,000 tax free to his children. In addition, there would be an exemption of $10,000 if left to one child. In that case $110,000 would be tax free. If the same principle were applied to an estate with a $100,000 minimum, no estate tax would be paid on estates far in excess of $100,000. I do not think that would be fair or just.
As a newcomer to this house, I feel that the changes put forward are very important. They show that parliament and democracy are really working. The people of Canada and hon. members from both sides of the house made recommendations. I think it is a great thing that some of these recommendations have been accepted. I have a recommendation to suggest which I feel would be worth while, particularly in my riding of Ontario. This area is 50 per cent rural. It is very close to metropolitan Toronto. As a consequence, the value of land has increased very sharply in the last few years. Some of these farmers wish to continue farming and their children wish to continue farming. Under the present legislation, their farms would be assessed at real estate value rather than at farm value and there could be an excessive estate tax payable.
I suggest that the farm be assessed at both real estate and farm value. If the beneficiary of the estate guarantees that he or she intends to continue farming, then the estate tax should be payable at the farm value. If the farm is later sold the estate tax would become payable as originally assessed, at the real estate value plus interest. This would give farmers the right to continue farming in areas of great increases in values of land. I think this plan is workable. It may sound complicated from an administrative standpoint, but I do not believe this. At the time of the death and the assessment of the property, the government could put a lien on the property for the difference in estate tax payable as between farm and real estate values. This lien would be held until such time as the property is sold. Such a practice would be a step toward helping farmers in my particular area.
Looking at the new proposals in detail, I am impressed with the social implications of this new estate tax. It is a step in the right direction to recognize the principle that both a husband and wife contribute to the value of

This is being done by allowing an exemption of $10,000 per adult child, plus an exemption for non-adult children of $1,000 per year between the ages of 1 and 26. What about the negative views that have been expressed? First of all, the argument has been put forward by some on the opposition side that a person has earned his money so there should be no tax on it whatsoever, and that, in particular, there should be no such thing as estate tax. I do not think that is a valid point. If we carried that practice through for a number of years we would end up with the wealth of the nation amassed in the hands of far too few people. We have to find a happy medium whereby we can redistribute the wealth and at the same time recognize it is important that people have incentives to earn money and to save it. This kind of legislation recognizes the needs of both levels.
Let us look at the implications of the estate tax in practice. I think I pointed out earlier that many people seem to feel that estate tax is a new kind of tax in Canada. Mr. Speaker, after listening to the speeches on the estate tax, I am pleased, in turn, to say a few words.
I should like to give my point of view on the new rules concerning the proposed amendments to the Estate Tax Act. I shall not go into details, because several hon. members have done so.
Briefly, I would like to say that corporations do not die but individuals do. The law under consideration affects individuals, the small corporations, the small companies whose president holds almost all the shares. When the president of such a small company dies, it is subject to the same laws and regulations as the individual, including the Estate Tax Act. Mr. Speaker, under that act and its regulations, we will continue to undermine private enterprise and free enterprise.
Mr. Speaker, free enterprise will no longer exist in a few years, for even if the bill contains some desirable tax exemptions, such exemptions are not considerable if one realizes that $100,000 are not worth today what that same amount was worth 50 years ago. In fact, a $100,000 or $200,000 estate is negligible today, since money is valueless now.
I was saying that corporations do not die. The large corporations that operate with the help of millions of dollars cannot be taxed, and since they will never die, in consequence, they will never pay. Once again, the small estates, the small businessmen will pay the piper, will be thrown in the street, in short will disappear to leave only the large corporations and state organizations which can enjoy privileges denied to small companies.
It is basically unfair, in my opinion, to tax individuals more than corporations. There is no honest or serious reason to treat instruments better than individuals who use them,

consequently to treat corporations better than individuals.
Mr. Speaker, under this legislation, corporations should pay as much estate taxes as individuals. The mere fact that they are organized in a corporation does not entitle individuals to privileges, at the expense of isolated people in our society which collects taxes for its administration.

At this time I think I can be of no more service than to read several excerpts from some of the local papers in my area which reflect the opinion of people out that way. Let
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act me quote from the Wainwright Star-Chronicle as follows:
It doesn't take much of a farm these days to be worth $100,000, including everything. And those who operate this size of a farm are having a hard time to keep going. Thousands of them at this very moment are finding every cent of income is committed to paying bills-and there never seems to be enough to pay them all.

A cash reserve is non-existent under these Circumstances.
Almost three quarters of Canada's farmers have a taxable income of less than $4,000 a year; one in four has a taxable income between $4,000 and $10,000. Not much opportunity to build up cash reserves there, especially in the last few years. Yet the heirs of the farmer who leaves a farm valued at $100,000 must raise $17,400 to pay the estate tax on it. The same applies to many other types of small business enterprises, whose operators have a lot of money tied up in the enterprise, but have little ready cash and low net earnings.
If the farm is valued at $200,000-again not an unusually high figure these days-the heirs would have to raise $51,000 to pay the tax.
It is almost incredible that the government that has had so much to say about the "Just Society" should introduce such punitive legislation. It seems to us there could be no quicker way to destroy the family farm, and to hasten the day when land resources will be controlled by huge corporations.
The following is another excerpt from another prairie publication which reads:
It seems strange to me that in these times when so much emphasis is being put on maintaining family farms and family units both by the government and farm organizations that we would be faced with such a bill as the new estate tax proposal. We seem to be trying to make the tail wag the dog and this never works for very long. It looks like a pretty short term outlook to me. Commercial agriculture just can't stand estate taxes; farmers and ranchers have been having enough of a struggle as it is to keep in business and the proposed tax would mean every generation would have to start all over again and everyone knows this is impossible in agriculture. It isn't an in-and-outers game but a business that takes years to build. If you can't turn your business over to your heirs there really isn't much point in having a business at all. If the proposed bill is approved by Parliament a guy with a ranch might as well sell out rather than try to build an outfit to pass along to his sons because it looks to me like he will just be putting them in debt for the rest of their lives and when and if they do ever own the thing they won't be able to pass it on to their sons anyway. Just looking at the thing from a farmer's viewpoint it seems to me some very careful thought and consideration better be put into this estate tax bill before they ever consider approving it. This can do more harm to agriculture than anything I know of. Agriculture has to have continuity and this idea of a double taxation surely is the wrong approach.
In the past, the people of Canada have been led to believe that the Liberal party of

In my opinion, and not only in my opinion but also in the opinions of tens of thousands of Canadians today, the Minister of Finance is aligning himself solidly with the socialist doctrine that all wealth belongs to the state. He is accepting one of the proposals in the Carter Commission report that has been advocated for so long by our friends in the New Democratic Party.
The hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre), when he spoke yesterday, deplored amassed wealth and referred to the Rockefellers, the Krupps and the Duponts. He would have us believe that the new estate tax proposals would remedy all this and that all wealth would be equalized. Absolutely the opposite is the case. We are working on an entirely different group of people here. I remind you that the estate tax affects only 50 per cent of the real wealth of the nation, whereas it used to tax 54 per cent. On estates in the million dollar class, the reduction, in estate tax has been 4 per cent. We might go on to look at the equity of the social development tax, according to which a man who has an income of $4,000 to $8,000 is being taxed at the same rate as the man who makes $1 million. Certainly, there is nothing here that would indicate that the minister is doing something to distribute the real wealth of the country.
I must congratulate the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) on his suggestion with regard to the assessment of land because, as I see it, this is one of the real inequalities. He mentioned that there should be one taxation rate on real estate and he gave an example of the way in which the encroachment of cities pushes up land values. He thought it would be a good idea to assess land on the basis of farm values. I would certainly go along with this suggestion. In my area a great many farms may be valued at $100,000 according to present inflated land values but in actual fact the net return on them may be less than $2,500 a year. This was the figure given by the Economic Council of Canada as being at the poverty level.
These people cannot keep a property of this kind and pay these estate taxes. If we allow the discontinuance of farming that will have an effect on the employment situation. If farmers who are forced off the farm are employable, someone else will be out of a job.

We have only to look at some of the provinces today to realize that in at least one of them the unemployment figure is reaching over 10 per cent.

At current market prices which are artificially high because of the pressures brought to bear by many factors-and I would use as examples hobby farmers, foreign corporations and Hutterite colonies- the value of the land is vastly over-rated.
